changes.before: These six commitments help you see whether equity is meaningfully built into a plan. If one is missing, return to that part of the work before moving ahead.
changes.after: Use these commitments to examine how a plan distributes responsibility, influence, and the work of participation. A gap may require a change in the plan itself, such as involving people before a decision is settled or explaining how their input will be used.

changes.before: Center lived experience: people affected by a decision should help shape it, with their role, authority, and compensation made clear.
changes.after: Center lived experience: people affected by a decision should help shape it. Explain their role, what they can influence, who holds decision-making authority, and what compensation is available so they can decide whether and how to participate.

changes.before: Move at the speed of trust: build relationships and explain how input was used before expanding the work. Rebuilding trust after a rushed launch takes time.
changes.after: Build trust over time: develop relationships and explain what happened with people’s input before expanding the work. Include what changed, what did not change, and why; an invitation to participate is not by itself evidence that the relationship is working.

changes.before: Name access assumptions early: broadband, a printer, English literacy, a car, daytime availability, or a phone that takes calls. Each assumption can keep someone from taking part.
changes.after: Identify access assumptions while the design is still open. A service may depend on broadband, a printer, English literacy, a car, daytime availability, or a phone that accepts calls. Examine which of these conditions are necessary and what alternative is available when a person cannot meet them.

changes.before: Before creating an online option, decide how people can get help by phone, on paper, or in person. Make sure staff are available to support those options.
changes.after: Plan phone, paper, or in-person help alongside an online option, and identify the staff needed to provide it. A listed alternative offers little practical access if the people who need it cannot reach someone able to help.

changes.before: Use it as a working document for your program, with a responsible person for each follow-up and a review date. This makes the next steps clear and accountable.
changes.after: Use the checklist to connect each finding with a responsible person, a next step, and a review date. Its value lies in what it helps the team examine and change; completing the checklist alone does not establish that an access barrier has been resolved.

changes.before: The wrong dialect, an unreviewed translation, or an English-only exception process can keep people from receiving meaningful access.
changes.after: Availability on paper does not establish usable language access. The wrong dialect, an unreviewed translation, or an English-only route to request help can leave a person unable to understand or respond, even when the program has interpretation or translation arrangements.

changes.before: Written material: plain language first; then translation. A dense English notice becomes a dense translated notice.
changes.after: Written material: clarify the purpose, meaning, and next step in the original document before translation. Translation changes the language; it does not by itself resolve confusing instructions or a poorly organized notice.

changes.before: If a person cannot read or use a notice, they may not be able to understand or appeal the decision. Accessibility needs to be addressed before release.
changes.after: A notice may contain accurate information and still be difficult to read or use. If the reader cannot understand the decision or how to respond, their opportunity to act or appeal may be affected. Review meaning and accessibility together before release.

changes.before: Timing: evening or weekend options for working people; religious observance and school calendars checked; enough notice.
changes.after: Timing: ask what meeting times are workable, including evening or weekend options where appropriate. Check religious observances and school calendars, and give enough notice for people to arrange participation; a date that works for staff may not work for those invited.

changes.before: Payment and follow-up: explain whether people will be paid and when they will hear what changed.
changes.after: Payment and follow-up: explain whether people will be paid and when they will hear what happened with their input. Include changes made, decisions that remained the same, and the reasons, so participants can understand the response.
